event.text: Write an essay of about 400 words on the history of lighthouses. Do not use any tools.

# A Brief History of Lighthouses

For as long as people have sailed, they have needed a way to find the shore safely in darkness. The earliest solutions were simple: bonfires lit on hilltops and headlands, tended by those who lived near dangerous coasts. Over time these fires were raised onto platforms and towers to make them visible from farther out, and the lighthouse was born.

The most famous ancient example was the Pharos of Alexandria, completed around 280 BCE under the Ptolemaic rulers of Egypt. Standing perhaps a hundred metres tall, it was among the tallest structures of the ancient world and one of its Seven Wonders. A fire at its summit, possibly amplified by polished metal mirrors, guided ships into the busy harbour for well over a thousand years before earthquakes finally brought it down. The Romans carried the idea across their empire, building towers at Ostia, Dover, and La Coruña, where the Tower of Hercules still stands and remains in service.

After Rome's decline, lighthouse building largely lapsed in Europe. Coastal lights were often kept by monks or local communities, and were modest and unreliable. The revival came with the growth of maritime trade from the late medieval period onward. France's Cordouan lighthouse, finished in 1611, combined engineering ambition with palatial decoration.

The eighteenth century brought the challenge of building on exposed offshore rocks. The Eddystone reef off Plymouth saw a succession of towers: Henry Winstanley's wooden structure was swept away in the Great Storm of 1703, and its successor burned. John Smeaton's 1759 tower, built of interlocking granite blocks with a curved profile modelled on an oak trunk, set the pattern for rock lighthouses thereafter. In Scotland, the Stevenson family built dozens of remarkable lights, including Bell Rock and Skerryvore.

Illumination improved alongside construction. Open coal fires and candles gave way to oil lamps, and the Argand lamp of the 1780s produced a steadier, brighter flame. The decisive advance came in 1822, when Augustin-Jean Fresnel devised a lens of concentric prisms that gathered light into a powerful, concentrated beam visible for many miles. Fresnel lenses spread worldwide, and distinctive flash patterns let mariners identify individual lights.

The twentieth century brought electricity, radio beacons, and finally automation. Keepers, once emblematic of solitary devotion, were gradually withdrawn; the last manned lighthouse in the United Kingdom was automated in 1998. Satellite navigation has since reduced the lighthouse's practical importance, yet many remain lit as backups, and others survive as museums, lodgings, and cherished landmarks — enduring symbols of guidance and safety.
